comment: Every status claim in README.md's Features table resolves to an entry here.
`scripts/readme-status-gate.js` parses that table and fails when a status cell is not a vocabulary word
allowed here, when the word is stronger than the evidence recorded against the feature, or when a feature
The vocabulary is deliberately weak. `tested` says a test exists that exercises the feature; it does not say
the feature is correct. `verified` is reserved for a claim backed by an artifact this project produced and
can be pointed at — and it is withheld where an audit has found the opposite.
Rules learned the hard way in this repository: a benchmark figure without a citation, and an install command
that returns 404, both shipped for months because nothing checked the text against the evidence.

The five defects that made the fixture pass are fixed; the package-name resolver is what makes the claim true for a released dependency.

Taint Analysis.evidence: benchmarks/owasp-benchmark.json, produced by .github/workflows/owasp-benchmark.yml from OWASP-Benchmark/BenchmarkJava at commit f40c618: 2740 labelled cases, 1415 real vulnerabilities, TPR 0.9258, FPR 0.0000, score 0.9258. The engine is scored in two halves over the same corpus: the flow analysis alone scores 0.5633 (TPR 0.5633, FPR 0.0000) and the rule family alone 0.3625 (TPR 0.3625, FPR 0). Over the seven flow categories the flow subset scores 0.8836 (TPR 0.8836, FPR 0.0000). All eleven categories are at FPR 0.0000, so the engine reports no safe case in the corpus at all. Acceptance suite: tests/e2e/owasp-benchmark.test.ts (7 cases: a named vulnerable case, a named escaped one, a named file write that must not read as cross-site scripting, named cases for three of the four rule categories, and a repeat-run determinism check), plus packages/intelligence/src/__tests__/call-result-end-to-end.test.ts (5 cases through JavaProvider: a helper that returns its argument, one that never reads it, one that escapes it, one that hides it in a collection, and one the provider cannot read) callee-source-end-to-end.test.ts (4 cases for the generative direction) and container-round-trip-end-to-end.test.ts (4 cases: a map round trip that delivers the value to a read under its own key and not to one under another, a list shuffled by `add`/`remove` where the shifted position decides the answer, a `StringBuilder` read through `toString`, and the safe value written where the tainted one was read from). and discarded-value-end-to-end.test.ts (5 cases: a copy-wrap-cut chain that ends in a call on a constant and must stay quiet, the same chain with the value passed to the call and reporting, the chain ending in a constant that is never handed to anything, a value handed to `store(param)` where the return is a value the file cannot decide and the answer is therefore "cannot say", and the same shape where the return is a constant the file does decide). shadowed-name-end-to-end.test.ts (3 cases: the corpus's two-loop shape where the sink reads the loop's own declaration and must stay quiet, the same file with the sink moved into the loop that read the request and reporting, and one declaration read in two sibling loops where the flow must survive), binding-resolver.test.ts (6 cases for the resolver: a single binding, a name the function does not declare, two sibling declarations, an inner shadow, a declaration outside every region, and a grammar that reads no scopes), and sink-vocabulary-end-to-end.test.ts (5 cases: a value reaching `response.getWriter().printf(param)` reported as `html`, the same call with a constant format string reporting nothing, `JDBCtemplate.queryForRowSet(sql)` reported as `sql_exec`, three more `JdbcTemplate` spellings reported through their own files, and a constant SQL string reporting nothing). **The acceptance suite now reproduces the artifact exactly rather than staying under a bound.** It had been scoring a weaker engine since `constants` and `returnLines` were added to the workflow script and never to the suite: both are optional facts that are neutral when absent, so the suite measured an engine two models behind the published one while asserting floors (FPR ≤ 0.31) loose enough that the gap could not show. It now passes the same five facts the script passes and compares true and false positive counts against `benchmarks/owasp-benchmark.json`, so the two wirings are one wiring.
Taint Analysis.note: The four categories a flow cannot answer now have a rule family of their own, and they are why the score moved 0.1695 -> 0.4479: 513 of 513 vulnerable cases found across crypto, hash, weakrand and securecookie, at a false-positive rate of 0. Two of the rules read the project's own configuration, because the corpus selects its algorithm with `benchmark.properties` (`hashAlg1=MD5`) rather than at the call. **A `write` is not one sink**: the vocabulary matched a method name, and a method name names no destination, so 85 safe `Crypto` cases were charged for writing ciphertext into a file whose path was fixed when the writer was constructed. Filtering `html` sinks by the receiver's declared type moved the score 0.4479 -> 0.5128. **The defect that dominated the flow half was reachability, not vocabulary**: 151 of the 403 false positives contained the corpus's constant-condition dead branch (`bar = (7 * 18) + num > 200 ? "constant" : param` with `num = 106`), and the same construct appears in the vulnerable cases with the arms swapped, so both directions had to be answered. Constant folding plus a reachability fact on the CFG moved the score 0.5128 -> 0.6864, FPR 0.3042 -> 0.1306, with 1 156 true positives before and after and every category's FPR halved. The remaining 173 false positives are mostly cross-class: 170 of them call a helper (`doSomething`, `getTheValue`) whose returned value the single-file model cannot follow across the class boundary. **The remaining false positives were cross-class, and asking the callee answered the largest group.** `bar = helper(param)` was read as "the statement read a tainted name and wrote one", which is sound and useless once a getter or an escaping wrapper sits between the input and the sink; `return-summary.ts` asks the callee instead, per argument position, and the pipeline applies the answer as a verdict on the definition edge. Three defects had to be fixed before it worked and each produced a plausible number: the def->use index was keyed by statement rather than binding (so two parameters on one signature line answered for each other), the verdict was looked up by the binding the statement writes rather than the one carrying the value, and "no return reads this parameter" was given for arguments that vanished into `map.put` — which silenced 104 real vulnerabilities until `lost` was recorded. Measured: score 0.6864 -> 0.7015, FPR 0.1306 -> 0.1155, 1 156 true positives before and after, `xss` alone moving 0.2105 -> 0.1148 (44 -> 24 false positives). **The same summary carries the generative direction** — a callee that reads the input itself becomes a source in its caller — and no case in this corpus has such a callee (809 functions checked), so that half is evidenced by tests rather than by a figure. **The escaping vocabulary was wrong in two directions at once.** `HtmlUtils.htmlEscape` — Spring's escaper — was absent, so 11 safe `xss` cases were charged for escaping their own output; and the matcher tested `text.endsWith(name)` for every entry, which for a one-word entry is a suffix test, so `htmlUnescape`, `unescape` and `jsonUnescape` all matched the `escape` entry and a call that puts the danger back was read as removing it. Measured: score 0.7015 -> 0.7098, FPR 0.1155 -> 0.1072, `xss` alone 0.1148 -> 0.0622 (24 -> 13 false positives), 1 156 true positives before and after. The suffix rule's delta on this corpus is zero, which is stated rather than hidden: it is fixed because it is wrong, and held by a test rather than by a figure. **The 142 remaining false positives were then opened one at a time, and 141 of them put the value into a container and take it out again** — 79 through `map.put`/`get`, 62 through `list.add`/`get` and one through neither. The list half is the harder one because the corpus shuffles the value before reading it (`add`, `add(param)`, `add`, `remove(0)`, `get(1)`), so an answer needs what each index holds rather than what the collection holds. That is a model rather than a filter, and it was built: `container-flow.ts` keeps, per receiver, a map from literal key to the writers of that slot, and turns a read into **uses** of the statement that read it - so `bar = map.get("keyB")` becomes an ordinary def->use edge from `param` to `bar` and nothing downstream needs to know a container was involved. The guarantee it states - every access this function makes is a call on a binding, keys literal throughout, so the container holds exactly the values written under those keys - is what lets a read give a *negative* answer, which is what `ReturnSummary.lost` had been waiting for. Three defects were fixed on the way and each produced a plausible number: the operations table as an object literal (a `toString` key overrides `Object.prototype.toString`, widens `role` to `string` and stops compiling, and `in` answers true for four inherited names), a container's kind decided by the method name rather than by the key's shape (`get(0)` is a position, `get("keyA")` is a key), and an unknown method read as the container escaping rather than mutating - which made every `StringBuilder` chain in the corpus unfollowable and left 16 false positives exactly where they were. One state was added and deleted: gating `followed` on every read being exact measured identically to gating it on escape alone (1 207 true and 40 false positives both ways), so it was removed rather than kept for its look. Measured: score 0.7098 -> 0.8228, FPR 0.1072 -> 0.0302, true positives 1 156 -> 1 207 - 102 cases left the false-positive set, none entered it, none were lost and 51 were gained. Every category's FPR fell except `xpathi`: `trustbound` 0.2326 -> 0.0000, `ldapi` 0.2812 -> 0.0312, `pathtraver` 0.3185 -> 0.1037, `sqli` 0.2026 -> 0.0517, `cmdi` 0.1360 -> 0.0480, `xss` 0.0622 -> 0.0191. **38 of the 40 that remained were one shape, and it was not a container**: the helper ended with `String bar = thing.doSomething(g14546)` where `g14546` is the constant `"barbarians_at_the_gate"` and `thing` comes from `ThingFactory.createThing()`. Three variants of one case located the mechanism rather than guessing it: keeping the call with a literal argument still reported, replacing the call with `String bar = g14546;` stopped the report, and replacing the return with the constant stopped it too - so the value was carried by the summary's `carry`. **The carry was not the defect; `lost` was.** The summary had already answered "no return reads this parameter", and then refused to use its own answer because a nested call in the chain had "lost" the value - and a nested call in `String e = new String(Base64.decodeBase64(Base64.encodeBase64(d.getBytes())))` loses nothing: the statement keeps the result in `e`, and the walk reaches `e` from the same definition. The fact that separates the two cases is whether a statement keeps the value it computes, read from the tree the way the branch ranges are (a statement whose first child is an assignment keeps its value; `map.put("k", param);` keeps nothing), carried as `FunctionCfg.discardedValueRegions`. A loss is now recorded only inside a discarded statement, and an absent fact still means every line may be discarding. Measured: score 0.8228 -> 0.8515, FPR 0.0302 -> 0.0015, 1 207 true positives before and after - 38 cases left the false-positive set, none entered it, none were lost. Deleting `lost` outright measures the same figures on this corpus, which is stated rather than hidden: the guard is kept because it is right about the shape the corpus does not contain, and `discarded-value-end-to-end.test.ts` holds both directions. **The last 2 were not a block question, and the previous round's answer to them was wrong**: `BenchmarkTest01479` and `BenchmarkTest02370` write `String value = values[i]` inside one loop and `Element value = nodeList.item(i)` inside another, and the claim that a single-block CFG made the first value reach the second sink was only half of it. A name is not a variable: the two declarations are two variables that share a spelling, and one binding per spelling carried the first one's taint to the second one's sink. Declarations now begin a variable and are separated by the scope each sits in (`ConstantDialect.scopeTypes`), a write inside an existing variable's own scope joins it, and a write in a scope the first one does not contain begins a new one - which is the rule that separates the corpus's two loops while keeping every assignment inside a `try` attached to the name the `try` is inside. **The naive form of that rule was measured and rejected**: keying the binding by `(name, scope)` made every assignment a declaration, split each variable into one binding per block, and cut 503 real vulnerabilities out of the report before the containment rule replaced it. Measured: score 0.8515 -> 0.8530, FPR 0.0015 -> 0.0000, 1 207 true positives before and after, 2 cases left the false-positive set, none entered it, none were lost - and every one of the eleven categories is now at FPR 0.0000, which is the first time the engine reports no safe case in the corpus. **The next 105 silent cases were not a modelling question at all, and two families of them were one missing word each.** A flow that reaches no name the vocabulary calls a sink is a vulnerability no analysis can report: `printf` was absent from `JAVA_SINKS` while `print`, `println` and `write` were present, and `PrintWriter.printf(format, args)` writes the same response body through the same receiver the destination filter had already approved (51 vulnerable `xss` cases); Spring's `JdbcTemplate` reaches a database through `queryForRowSet`, `queryForList`, `queryForMap`, `queryForObject`, `queryForLong` and `batchUpdate` rather than JDBC's `executeQuery` (52 `sqli` cases). Measured: score 0.8530 -> 0.9258, TPR 0.8530 -> 0.9258, FPR 0.0000 -> 0.0000, true positives 1 207 -> 1 310 - 103 gained, none lost, and not one of them a false positive. `xss` 0.6869 -> 0.8943, `sqli` 0.7463 -> 0.9375, `flows` (engine) 0.4905 -> 0.5633, and the rule family unchanged at 0.3625, which is the figure that says the move came from the flow half rather than from the rules. **`query` was not added to the Java table**: it is already in the shared list and the Java table is appended to it, so a second entry would be two spellings of one answer - and the run that removed it measures identically (1 310 true, 0 false), which is stated rather than assumed. What remains is 105 cases with no shared cause - `cmdi` 32, `xss` 26, `sqli` 17, `pathtraver` 15, `trustbound` 11, `ldapi` 3, `xpathi` 1 - and the largest group is `new ProcessBuilder().command(argList)` followed by `.start()`, where the command is handed over as a list the container model follows a value into but not out of the argument the container is built from.

Security Rule Families.evidence: benchmarks/owasp-benchmark.json > byEngine.rules: TPR 0.3625, FPR 0.0000, score 0.3625 over all 2740 cases; within the four categories the rules answer, 513 of 513 vulnerable and 0 of 529 safe. Acceptance suites: tests/e2e/owasp-benchmark.test.ts (two cases over the real corpus) and packages/intelligence/src/__tests__/security-rule-families.test.ts (30 cases, 99% statements and 98% branches). Gate: scripts/owasp-benchmark-gate.js holds every category at TPR 1.0 and the rule family's own FPR at 0.
Security Rule Families.note: Four rules for Java: weak-cipher, weak-hash, weak-random, insecure-cookie. They are a rule family rather than a flow because the bug is a property of a call — 'this program chose DES' — and no path analysis reaches it. `evaluateSecurityRules` takes configuration as an input, which is what makes it the first capability here that needs the index rather than one file: 258 of the corpus's hash and crypto cases name their algorithm through `getProperty`, and the answer is in `benchmark.properties`. Only Java is covered; `ruleCoverage()` reports that rather than letting an empty result read as clean.
